issues.title: 214(b): presumed to be leaving forever
issues.category_name: Visas, consulate queues and the money spent on being told no
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: US law presumes every visitor-visa applicant intends to immigrate. The applicant must disprove a presumption about his own mind. For Mexicans this single subsection is the overwhelming majority of refusals, and there is no appeal from it.

details.aspect: The presumption is the mechanism
details.description: Section 214(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act presumes intending immigration. The officer does not have to prove the applicant will overstay; the applicant has to prove he will not, which is a negative about the future.
details.energy_note: Proving what you are not going to do.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - how much of the refusal stream it is
details.description: Practitioner estimates put 214(b) at roughly 89% of all B-1/B-2 refusals issued to Mexican nationals at US consulates in Mexico. It is described as the most common US visa refusal in the world.
details.energy_note: Nine refusals in ten are this one clause.
details.notes: The 89% figure is from an immigration law firm, not State Department data. State publishes adjusted refusal rates by nationality annually; that is the citable source.

details.aspect: The fee is not returned
details.description: The MRV fee buys an interview, not a visa, and is not refunded on refusal. Reapplying means paying it again, with no waiting period required and no limit on attempts - and no reason to expect a different answer on the same evidence.
details.energy_note: Paying again for the same answer.

details.aspect: The 'weak ties' profile is the modern working life
details.description: Refusals cluster on: work that does not require physical presence (commission sales, gig work, remote contracting), renting rather than owning, and family who could plausibly relocate too. A young man with a laptop and a rented room is the profile.
details.energy_note: Punished for having a job that does not tie him to a building.

details.aspect: Money in the account is read against you either way
details.description: Too little and there are insufficient funds. A single large deposit and it looks arranged for the application. There is no published balance that suffices, because the standard is the officer's overall impression.
details.energy_note: No number he could have put in the account.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - the four-minute interview
details.description: He has the property deed, the employment letter, the bank statements and the return ticket. The officer asks three questions, none about any of it, and slides a blue sheet under the glass. Total elapsed time at the window: under four minutes. The queue behind him is 300 people long.
details.energy_note: Four minutes, and the folder never opened.

details.aspect: The refusal is remembered by the next officer
details.description: Prior refusals are visible in the system at every subsequent application, so a single 214(b) becomes a fact about him that he carries into every future interview, in any category.
details.energy_note: One no, quoted back at him for twenty years.

details.aspect: It is the hurdle the game should open with
details.description: For the Mexican difficulty setting this is the natural first gate: cheap to explain, instantly legible, and it produces the correct feeling - that he did everything asked and it did not matter.
details.energy_note: He did everything right. It did not matter.
details.notes: Design note for the journey scenes.

issues.title: The appointment that is eighteen months away
issues.category_name: Visas, consulate queues and the money spent on being told no
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Even a successful application is rationed by calendar. Post-pandemic backlogs at Mexican consulates reached multi-year waits, which converts a visa into a thing you plan your life around rather than apply for.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the peak backlog
details.description: Post-COVID, B1/B2 waits in Mexico reached nearly three years. By mid-2023 Ciudad Juárez and Guadalajara were showing first availability only in 2025.
details.energy_note: Apply now, be seen the year after next.

details.aspect: It recovered unevenly and is still long
details.description: By June 2025 the Mexico City average had dropped below 200 days, with Monterrey and Tijuana shorter in some weeks; other guidance still cited 300+ days into late 2025. Peak months are November-January and June-August.
details.energy_note: Better, and still most of a year.

details.aspect: The wait prices out the emergency
details.description: A funeral, a sick parent, a daughter's graduation, a contract that starts in March - none of these can wait 300 days, so the visa system is structurally unable to serve the reasons people most want to travel.
details.energy_note: By the time it comes through, the reason is over.

details.aspect: Consulate towns run on the queue
details.description: Ciudad Juárez has an economy built around people waiting: hotels, photo shops, form-fillers, notarios, medical exam clinics. The applicant pays all of it before he knows the answer.
details.energy_note: A whole town charging him while he waits to be refused.

issues.title: The ten-year bar you trigger by applying honestly
issues.category_name: Visas, consulate queues and the money spent on being told no
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Unlawful presence in the US creates a three- or ten-year bar on return. The bar is triggered by departing - so the man who leaves voluntarily to do it properly is the one who gets barred.

details.aspect: The trap in the design
details.description: Unlawful presence over 180 days triggers a 3-year bar; over a year, a 10-year bar. But the bar attaches on departure. Staying silently accrues no penalty you ever have to face; leaving to regularise is what activates it.
details.energy_note: Doing it properly is what gets you barred.

details.aspect: Which is why the consulate is in Ciudad Juárez
details.description: Immigrant visa interviews for Mexican applicants are consolidated at Ciudad Juárez. A man who has lived in Chicago for fifteen years must travel to a border city he may never have seen, to be interviewed, and may simply not be allowed back.
details.energy_note: Flown to a city he does not know, to find out if his life continues.

details.aspect: The waiver exists and is discretionary
details.description: The I-601A provisional waiver lets some applicants seek forgiveness of the bar before departing, on proof of extreme hardship to a qualifying US relative. Hardship to himself does not count, and 'extreme' is not defined by a number.
details.energy_note: His own ruin is not a qualifying hardship.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - the castigo
details.description: The word people use for it is *el castigo* - the punishment. His lawyer said it was the right thing to do. He is thirty-eight, his children are in Illinois, and a man behind glass in Juárez has just told him ten years. He asks whether there is an appeal. There is not.
details.energy_note: Ten years, said through glass, with no appeal.

issues.title: The border crossing card, and the line it draws
issues.category_name: Visas, consulate queues and the money spent on being told no
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The BCC/laser visa permits short visits within a limited zone. It is the most common US visa held by Mexicans and it is explicitly not permission to work, live, or go far inland.

details.aspect: A card that is geography, not status
details.description: It allows short stays within a limited distance of the border. Step beyond the zone or the day count and the lawful visit becomes a violation retroactively.
details.energy_note: Lawful here, unlawful thirty miles further on.

details.aspect: It is revocable at the bridge, without a hearing
details.description: An officer at the port of entry can cancel it on suspicion of work or intent to remain. There is no appeal; the card is simply cut or kept.
details.energy_note: Cancelled by one officer, in one minute.

details.aspect: Losing it costs the family income
details.description: For border households the card is the commute - to a shift, a market, a clinic. Cancellation is the loss of a job, not a trip.
details.energy_note: Not a holiday cancelled. A wage.

details.aspect: SCENE - thirty miles
details.description: He has crossed on the card four hundred times for the market. Today his cousin asks him to drop a toolbox in Tucson - seventy miles. He says no. His cousin does not understand why, and he cannot explain that the card is a radius rather than a permission.
details.energy_note: A permission shaped like a circle on a map.

issues.title: CURP, acta, and proving you were born
issues.category_name: Passport, CURP, acta de nacimiento: proving who you are
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Mexico, any gender
issues.summary: Mexican administrative life runs on the CURP and a certified birth certificate. A man whose birth was registered late, in another state, or with an inconsistent name spends years reconciling himself.

details.aspect: Everything requires it
details.description: Work, banking, school enrolment, health coverage, a phone contract and a passport all key off CURP and the acta. One mismatch propagates into all of them.
details.energy_note: One wrong letter, in every system at once.

details.aspect: Late registration is common and costly to fix
details.description: Rural and indigenous births registered late or informally produce adults whose documents disagree with each other. Correcting a civil registry entry is a judicial or administrative process, not a form.
details.energy_note: Going to court to prove your own birthday.

details.aspect: Two surnames, and systems that hold one
details.description: Mexican naming uses paternal and maternal surnames. Foreign systems store one, truncate, or swap them - so the same man is several different people across databases.
details.energy_note: Filed under four versions of his own name.
details.notes: See NAM-001.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - the accent that is not there
details.description: His acta says Martínez. The bank's system dropped the accent and the second surname years ago. The clerk says the names do not match and he will need a document proving he is himself. He asks which document proves that. She does not know.
details.energy_note: Asked to prove he is the person standing there.

issues.title: A passport that is fine, and a nationality that is the problem
issues.category_name: Passport, CURP, acta de nacimiento: proving who you are
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The Mexican passport is functional and reasonably ranked. The hurdle is not the booklet - it is that the nationality on it changes the question being asked at every counter.

details.aspect: The document works; the reading of it does not
details.description: Unlike the Iranian or Palestinian cases in the sibling datasets, the Mexican passport is not itself a broken instrument. What it triggers is a presumption about intent - see VIS-001 - rather than non-recognition.
details.energy_note: A good passport, read as a statement of intent.
details.notes: Deliberate contrast with assets/text/iran DOC-001 and assets/text/palestine, where the document itself fails.

details.aspect: Visa-free access is wide and hollow where it matters
details.description: Mexicans travel visa-free to much of Europe, Japan and South America. The single destination that matters most for family, work and money - the United States - is the one that requires the interview.
details.energy_note: Free to go almost everywhere except where his family is.

details.aspect: Renewal from abroad is its own problem
details.description: Consular appointments abroad are scarce, and an expiring passport abroad interacts with an expiring immigration status: the man may not be able to renew one without the other.
details.energy_note: Two documents, each requiring the other.

details.aspect: SCENE - the visa-free list
details.description: His passport takes him to Japan, Brazil, Germany and Turkey without asking anyone. It does not take him to the hospital in San Diego where his mother is. He has shown it at eleven borders and been refused at the only one that mattered.
details.energy_note: Eleven countries open, and the one with his mother closed.

issues.title: The papers you no longer have
issues.category_name: Passport, CURP, acta de nacimiento: proving who you are
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Deportation, detention and robbery strip people of the documents their subsequent life requires, at the exact moment they have least capacity to replace them.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - property not returned on removal
details.description: A University of Arizona survey of Mexicans deported from the US found 39% said American authorities did not return their belongings - leaving people without IDs, wallets or phones, unable to call anyone, access money, or prove identity to Mexican authorities on arrival.
details.energy_note: Handed back across the line with nothing in his pockets.

details.aspect: Arriving undocumented in your own country
details.description: Without ID he cannot claim the reception centre benefit, board a bus home, rent a room or start work - in the country of his own nationality.
details.energy_note: A Mexican with no way to prove he is Mexican.

details.aspect: Replacement requires the thing being replaced
details.description: Getting a new acta or CURP typically requires identification, which is the thing that is gone. The loop is resolved by someone's discretion, or not at all.
details.energy_note: Needs ID to get ID.

issues.title: The second room
issues.category_name: Airports abroad, screening and the second room
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Secondary inspection: referral out of the primary queue into a room with no clock, no phone and no lawyer. The brief asked specifically about unusually high rates of 'random checks' - this issue records what is actually documented and what is not.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the published referral rate
details.description: Of about 420 million travellers CBP processed at ports of entry in FY2024, 12,660,784 - roughly 3% - were referred to secondary inspection.
details.energy_note: Three in a hundred, officially.

details.aspect: Referral needs no suspicion at all
details.description: Officers at primary have broad discretion to refer with or without any suspicion of wrongdoing. Listed grounds include document issues, possible violations, an alert - and explicitly 'random screening' and 'officer discretion'.
details.energy_note: No reason is required, and none will be given.

details.aspect: THE HONEST GAP - no per-nationality rate is published
details.description: No government publishes a secondary-inspection rate broken down by nationality. The headline 3% also pools hundreds of millions of routine land crossings, so it says almost nothing about the rate for any specific profile. The disparity Mexicans report is consistent and unmeasured.
details.energy_note: Everyone reports it; nobody counts it.
details.notes: Same treatment as AIR-001 in assets/text/nigeria and the Palestine dataset. Recorded as a gap, not asserted.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - device searches are rarer than the fear of them
details.description: CBP searched the devices of 47,047 travellers in FY2024 - about 0.3% of those sent to secondary, under 0.01% of all arrivals - rising to roughly 55,000 in FY2025. About 90% were basic manual searches. CBP states device access is not a purpose of secondary referral.
details.energy_note: Rare, and it does not feel rare.

details.aspect: The cost is the connection, not the question
details.description: Two hours in the room means the onward flight, the shift, the hire car, the hotel night. Nobody reimburses any of it and no finding of wrongdoing is ever made.
details.energy_note: No charge, no apology, and the flight is gone.

details.aspect: It reshapes how he travels for the rest of his life
details.description: Arriving six hours early, never booking tight connections, carrying a folder of proof nobody asks for, flying on Tuesdays. An unpriced tax on every future journey.
details.energy_note: Six hours early, every time, for the rest of his life.

details.aspect: What the second room actually is
details.description: Rows of bolted chairs, no clock, phones surrendered or forbidden, no explanation of expected duration, and no one to ask. The design communicates that his time is not a cost to anybody.
details.energy_note: No clock on the wall, deliberately.

details.aspect: He will not mention it to the people meeting him
details.description: Explaining a four-hour delay to a waiting family means explaining being suspected, so most people say the flight was late.
details.energy_note: Tells them the flight was late.

issues.title: Your phone, at the border, without a warrant
issues.category_name: Airports abroad, screening and the second room
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The border search exception removes the warrant requirement. Messages, photographs, contacts and drafts are readable, and refusing costs more for a visa holder than for a citizen.

details.aspect: The legal position is settled and recent
details.description: CBP may conduct a basic manual search of phones, laptops and drives with no warrant and no individualised suspicion. Advanced forensic searches require reasonable suspicion under CBP Directive 3340-049A. In United States v. Eta (7th Cir., 2026) the court reaffirmed manual searches need neither warrant nor suspicion.
details.energy_note: Lawful, settled, and total.

details.aspect: The consequences of refusing are asymmetric
details.description: Citizens cannot be denied entry for refusing. Visa holders and border-crossing-card holders can be refused entry or have the device seized. So the right to refuse exists mainly for people who do not need it.
details.energy_note: He may refuse, and then not enter.

details.aspect: It reaches everyone he has ever messaged
details.description: The contents include other people's messages, photographs and numbers. None of them are present and none of them consented.
details.energy_note: His mother's messages, read in a room in Texas.

details.aspect: SCENE - unlock it
details.description: The officer holds out his hand for the phone. He thinks about the photographs of his daughter, the argument with his wife, his brother's messages about the paperwork. He unlocks it, because the alternative is not getting in, and stands there while a stranger scrolls.
details.energy_note: Watching a stranger read his marriage.

issues.title: Being the passenger the airline worries about
issues.category_name: Airports abroad, screening and the second room
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Carrier sanctions push the first check upstream: the airline decides at the gate whether it believes a passenger will be admitted, because the airline pays if he is not.

details.aspect: The airline is fined, so the airline screens
details.description: Carriers face penalties for bringing inadmissible passengers, so check-in staff apply their own risk assessment - with no obligation to explain and no appeal at the desk.
details.energy_note: Judged by a check-in agent on commercial risk.

details.aspect: Denied boarding is not denied entry, and costs the same
details.description: He has a valid visa and does not travel. There is no refusal on record to appeal, because no immigration officer ever saw him.
details.energy_note: Turned back before anyone official saw him.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - the supervisor is called
details.description: One-way ticket, cash purchase, a name the system renders two ways. The agent calls a supervisor, who looks at him rather than the screen, then says the flight is closed. It is not closed; boarding continues for twenty minutes.
details.energy_note: Told it was closed, watching it board.

issues.title: The deadliest land crossing in the world
issues.category_name: The border: crossing it, being turned around, dying on it
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The US-Mexico border is the most lethal overland migration route on record, and the lethality is a product of routing people into desert.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the count, and that it is a floor
details.description: IOM documented 686 deaths and disappearances on the US-Mexico border in 2022 - the deadliest land route worldwide on record, and nearly half of all 1,457 migrant deaths in the Americas that year. IOM states these are the lowest available estimates.
details.energy_note: Six hundred and eighty-six, counting low.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the desert does most of it
details.description: Nearly half - 307 - of the 2022 border deaths were linked to crossing the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts. For comparison, at least 212 people died in the Sahara that year.
details.energy_note: More died in the Sonoran than the Sahara.

details.aspect: The gaps in the count are named
details.description: IOM records that missing official data includes Texas border county coroners' offices and the Mexican search and rescue agency - so the undercount is specific and known, not vague.
details.energy_note: They can name which morgues do not report.

details.aspect: The price, and who holds it
details.description: Smuggling fees run into thousands of dollars, frequently borrowed against family land or paid to people connected to the groups who also run the kidnapping. The debt survives whether or not he arrives.
details.energy_note: The debt outlives the attempt.

details.aspect: Prevention through deterrence is the design, not the failure
details.description: Routing crossings away from urban corridors into desert was policy, on the reasoning that hostile terrain would deter. The deaths in BOR-001-002 are the predicted output of a chosen strategy rather than an accident of geography.
details.energy_note: The desert was the plan.

details.aspect: The remains that are never identified
details.description: A substantial share of recovered remains are never identified, so a family in Oaxaca has no death and no return - the same condition as DES-001, produced by a different mechanism.
details.energy_note: Not dead. Just never arrived.

issues.title: Turned around at the bridge
issues.category_name: The border: crossing it, being turned around, dying on it
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: A visa is permission to apply for entry, not permission to enter. The port-of-entry decision is final, unreviewable, and made in minutes.

details.aspect: CBP says so explicitly
details.description: A visa does not guarantee entry. Admissibility is determined at the port of entry by an officer, whose decision there is not subject to appeal.
details.energy_note: The visa was never a promise.

details.aspect: Withdrawal of application is offered as the kind option
details.description: Rather than a formal refusal, he may be offered the chance to withdraw his application for admission - which avoids a removal on his record and is also an agreement not to contest anything.
details.energy_note: Offered the merciful version, which is also a waiver.

details.aspect: Expedited removal leaves a five-year bar
details.description: The alternative to withdrawal can be expedited removal, carrying a bar on return, decided by an officer without a judge.
details.energy_note: Five years, decided at a counter.

details.aspect: SCENE - withdrawing the application
details.description: Four hours at the bridge. The officer offers him a form: sign, go home, no removal on the record. Or contest it, and risk a five-year bar. He signs. The visa in his passport is still valid and still worth nothing.
details.energy_note: A valid visa, and a signature saying he withdraws.

issues.title: Coming home, and the desk at that end too
issues.category_name: The border: crossing it, being turned around, dying on it
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Mexican customs and the return leg have their own discretion - the aduana button, the vehicle inspection, and the question of what he is bringing back.

details.aspect: The random light
details.description: Mexican customs uses a randomiser - press the button, green or red. Red means full inspection. It is genuinely random, which does not make it cheap when it happens.
details.energy_note: A red light and two hours.

details.aspect: Goods brought home are taxed as imports
details.description: The television, the tools, the things bought to bring back are subject to duty above the traveller allowance - so the savings of working abroad are partly taxed at the door.
details.energy_note: Taxed on the things he bought to bring home.

details.aspect: The vehicle with foreign plates
details.description: Cars brought in from the US require permits and deposits, and the regularisation rules change between administrations - so the legality of the car in the driveway is a moving target.
details.energy_note: A legal car that became illegal by decree.

details.aspect: SCENE - the red light
details.description: Twenty-two hours of driving, three hundred kilos of tools and gifts, and the button turns red. The inspector is polite and thorough and takes ninety minutes. Nothing is wrong. The television is charged duty because the receipt is in dollars.
details.energy_note: Ninety minutes, nothing wrong, and duty on the television.

issues.title: Put down in a dangerous city, after dark
issues.category_name: Deportation, removal and being put down somewhere at night
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Deportation is not only removal; it is a delivery, to a specific place, at a specific hour. Newly deported men are a preferred target for kidnapping and extortion, and the timing of release is what makes them findable.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - it has been counted
details.description: Over a six-week period in October to early December, Médecins Sans Frontières documented 1,267 people deported into Reynosa after dark, 588 of them after 8pm.
details.energy_note: Twelve hundred people, released into the dark.

details.aspect: The handover itself creates the exposure
details.description: After release from detention, people are processed by CBP at the international bridge, received by Mexican authorities, then moved to a returnee processing centre - a sequence that can take over three hours, leaving them visible and stationary late at night.
details.energy_note: Three hours standing in the open, visibly newly deported.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - MSF named the practice
details.description: MSF's head of mission for Mexico and Central America described 'dumping people in dangerous cities which they don't know after dark' as making an already traumatic process needlessly more damaging.
details.energy_note: The word the aid agency used was dumping.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - one in five arrive in the night hours
details.description: A University of Arizona survey found one in five Mexicans deported from the US reported being repatriated between 10pm and 5am, when services are closed.
details.energy_note: Arriving at the hour when nothing is open.

details.aspect: Tamaulipas is not an incidental destination
details.description: State Department reporting recorded Tamaulipas as having the highest kidnapping rate of any Mexican state, with Mexico's national public security system recording 887 kidnapping cases there in eight months of 2013. Reynosa's homicide rate has risen with conflict between criminal groups.
details.energy_note: Delivered to the state with the most kidnappings.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the shelter that locks people in
details.description: Reynosa became dangerous enough that, rather than deportees being locked out of a shelter during the day as is usual, they were locked in.
details.energy_note: The shelter locks the door from the outside, to protect them.

details.aspect: The shelter is full and the bus station is where you sleep
details.description: Capacity in border-city shelters is finite and arrivals are not scheduled to match it, so the overflow sleeps in public - visible, stationary and newly deported.
details.energy_note: Sleeping where everyone can see he has just arrived.

details.aspect: And he will try again within the week
details.description: For a man with citizen children in Illinois, the deportation is an obstacle rather than an ending, which is why DEP-002 records that most decline the ride south.
details.energy_note: Back at the line on Thursday.

issues.title: Lateral repatriation: sent back somewhere you have never been
issues.category_name: Deportation, removal and being put down somewhere at night
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Being returned not to where you crossed or where you are from, but to whichever port is operationally convenient - which can be two thousand kilometres from anyone who knows you.

details.aspect: The practice
details.description: Mexicans deported from the US are dropped off all along the border, in cities US officials describe as safer than the alternatives - but not necessarily near home, and not necessarily anywhere he has been before.
details.energy_note: Returned to his country, two thousand kilometres from it.

details.aspect: Getting home is his own problem and he has no money
details.description: The bus fare from a border city to a southern state is real money, which he does not have, having had his belongings not returned (DOC-003).
details.energy_note: A day and a half on a bus he cannot pay for.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the offer of a ride home is mostly declined
details.description: Ten Mexican reception centres reported 12,200 overnight stays and 9,300 debit cards issued, but only about 2,000 accepted free transport back to their home states - most do not take the ride south, because they intend to try again.
details.energy_note: Nine thousand helped, two thousand going home.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - the bridge at 11pm
details.description: The gate opens, six men walk through, and it closes. No phone, no belt, no laces, and $4 in coins between them. A car has been parked across the street the whole time, and it starts its engine.
details.energy_note: The car across the road starts its engine.

issues.title: The family that stays behind the line
issues.category_name: Deportation, removal and being put down somewhere at night
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Removal separates a household across a border one half cannot cross and the other half cannot re-enter, indefinitely.

details.aspect: The children are usually citizens
details.description: US-citizen children of a removed parent can visit but cannot relocate without giving up their schooling and their mother's work. The household simply operates in two countries.
details.energy_note: His daughter can visit him. He cannot attend her graduation.

details.aspect: He becomes a voice on a phone
details.description: Parenting continues by video call across a time difference, with his authority steadily reduced to money sent and advice given about a place he is no longer in.
details.energy_note: A father who exists mainly as a screen.

details.aspect: The income goes with him
details.description: Where he was the earner, removal converts a working household into a remittance-dependent one, or into poverty, immediately.
details.energy_note: One morning, and the household income is gone.

details.aspect: Trying to return is now a felony
details.description: Illegal re-entry after removal is a federal criminal offence, so the man who goes back to his children is prosecutable rather than merely removable.
details.energy_note: Going back to his kids is now a crime with a sentence.

details.aspect: SCENE - the Tuesday video call
details.description: His daughter holds the phone too close and shows him her spelling test. He says he is proud. She asks when he is coming. He says soon, which is what he said in March, and she has stopped asking follow-up questions about it.
details.energy_note: She has stopped asking when, which is worse.

issues.title: Served, then deported
issues.category_name: Deported veterans: served, then removed
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Lawful permanent residents who served in the US military, were told service meant citizenship, and were removed anyway - frequently for offences connected to untreated service injuries.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Bunker
details.description: The Deported Veterans Support House in Tijuana - 'the Bunker' - was founded in 2013 by Hector Barajas, a deported former 82nd Airborne paratrooper, after he began meeting homeless deported US veterans in the city. It is part shelter, part advocacy office, in a two-storey building attached to a tyre shop, with portraits of deported servicemen up the staircase.
details.energy_note: A shelter for men who served, run by one of them.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Barajas on the name
details.description: 'We call it the Bunker here because ... this is kind of like ... our place for us to be safe.'
details.energy_note: Safe, in the country they were sent to.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the scale is unknown and the known cases are many
details.description: Barajas estimated around 40 veterans had passed through the Bunker by 2016; by 2017 he had identified 350 deported US veterans born in more than 30 countries. Advocates believe there may be thousands worldwide. No government publishes the number.
details.energy_note: Nobody official counts them.

details.aspect: The belief that service conferred citizenship
details.description: Many at the Bunker said that when they enlisted they were led to believe naturalisation would be automatic. Most came to the US as children and were lawful permanent residents when they served.
details.energy_note: He thought the uniform had already made him one.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - a pardon is what it took
details.description: Barajas was able to become a US citizen only after a pardon from California Governor Jerry Brown in 2018. He later helped open a support house in the Dominican Republic.
details.energy_note: It took a governor's pardon to undo it.

details.aspect: Benefits he is still owed, in a country he cannot enter
details.description: VA healthcare entitlements frequently survive removal in principle while being unreachable in practice, since receiving them requires being in the United States.
details.energy_note: Entitled to care he would have to break the law to collect.

details.aspect: The flag on the wall
details.description: The Bunker is decorated with US flags and portraits of deported servicemen in uniform, with medals, discharge papers and photographs collaged on the walls - men asserting an allegiance to a country that has formally removed them.
details.energy_note: Saluting a flag that deported him.

details.aspect: Buried there, admitted here
details.description: Deported veterans frequently remain eligible for burial in a US national cemetery - so the state that would not let them live there will accept them once dead. This is the single most quotable fact in the dataset.
details.energy_note: Allowed back across the line in a coffin.

issues.title: The undocumented years
issues.category_name: Status in the US: the undocumented years, DACA, the waiting
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Living and working for a decade or more with no status: paying tax, raising citizens, and being removable at any moment for the whole period.

details.aspect: There is frequently no line to join
details.description: For a Mexican adult with no close US-citizen relative and no employer petition, no queue exists at all. 'Getting in line' describes a line that was never built for him.
details.energy_note: Told to wait in a queue that does not exist.

details.aspect: Taxes paid into systems that will never pay out
details.description: Work under an ITIN or a borrowed number contributes to Social Security and Medicare against a record he can never claim.
details.energy_note: Paying into a pension belonging to nobody.

details.aspect: Every ordinary risk is doubled
details.description: A traffic stop, a hospital admission, a dispute with a landlord or a wage complaint all carry a second consequence nobody else faces, which is why they go unreported.
details.energy_note: He cannot afford to be the victim of a crime.

details.aspect: The decade produces roots and no status
details.description: Fifteen years produces a mortgage, a business, school runs and citizen children - and not one day of lawful presence. Time accrues equity everywhere except in the file.
details.energy_note: Fifteen years of life, and zero days of status.

details.aspect: SCENE - fourteen years of W-2s
details.description: He keeps them in a shoebox: fourteen years of tax documents under a number that is not his. His lawyer says they prove good moral character and continuous presence. They also prove fourteen years of using a false number. The same box is the evidence both ways.
details.energy_note: The same shoebox is his defence and his confession.

issues.title: Status that can be cancelled by announcement
issues.category_name: Status in the US: the undocumented years, DACA, the waiting
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: DACA, TPS and parole are revocable programmes rather than status. People build lives on them and the ground can be withdrawn by policy change rather than by anything they did.

details.aspect: Renewable, and therefore never finished
details.description: Protection runs in short renewable terms with fees each time, so the holder is permanently within a year or two of an expiry date.
details.energy_note: Safe until the renewal, forever.

details.aspect: Registering is the condition and the risk
details.description: The programme requires handing over address, biometrics and family details, which is protective while the programme exists and is a locator list if it ends.
details.energy_note: The application is also a map to his front door.

details.aspect: Litigation means the future is decided elsewhere
details.description: Whether he can work next year is determined by appellate courts in cases he is not a party to and cannot influence.
details.energy_note: His life, on a docket he is not named in.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - the news alert at work
details.description: He is on a ladder when his phone buzzes. A court has ruled. He reads it twice, then keeps working, because there is nothing else to do with the information and the job finishes Thursday.
details.energy_note: Reads it twice, and carries on plastering.

issues.title: Detained, with no right to a lawyer
issues.category_name: Status in the US: the undocumented years, DACA, the waiting
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Immigration detention is civil, not criminal - which means no public defender, no right to appointed counsel, and detention in a facility that may be a thousand miles from any family.

details.aspect: Civil proceedings, criminal conditions
details.description: Because removal is a civil matter, there is no right to appointed counsel. Detainees are held in jails and contracted facilities regardless.
details.energy_note: Jailed by a process that is officially not punishment.

details.aspect: Representation changes outcomes enormously and costs money
details.description: Represented respondents fare dramatically better than unrepresented ones, so the outcome correlates with whether the family could raise a retainer that week.
details.energy_note: The verdict tracks the size of the retainer.

details.aspect: Transfer breaks the case and the visits
details.description: Detainees are moved between facilities and states, separating them from counsel, evidence and family without notice.
details.energy_note: Moved overnight, and the lawyer is now in another state.

details.aspect: Bond is set in money he does not have
details.description: Where bond is available at all it is set in thousands of dollars, so the difference between waiting outside and waiting inside is simply cash.
details.energy_note: Liberty, priced.

details.aspect: SCENE - the facility in another state
details.description: His wife drives six hours to the visit. When she arrives they tell her he was transferred on Friday to a facility in Louisiana. Nobody called her. Nobody called the lawyer either, and the hearing is Thursday.
details.energy_note: Six hours each way, to be told he left on Friday.

issues.title: The visa that belongs to the employer
issues.category_name: Work abroad: wage theft, the sponsor, the day-labour corner
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: H-2A and H-2B visas are tied to a single employer. Leaving a bad job means leaving the country, which is the entire leverage.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - almost every worker suffers a violation
details.description: Centro de los Derechos del Migrante's 'Ripe for Reform' found every H-2A worker interviewed suffered at least one serious legal violation, and 94% experienced three or more. 43% of 100 workers surveyed said their pay was less than promised during recruitment in Mexico.
details.energy_note: Ninety-four per cent, three violations or more.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the debt arrives before the job does
details.description: Despite recruitment fees being illegal under both US and Mexican law, CDM's 'Recruitment Revealed' found 58% of surveyed workers paid one. At the consulate a State Department official asks whether a fee was paid - by which point many are already deeply in debt because of it.
details.energy_note: Asked at the window whether he paid the fee he has already paid.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - enforcement finds violations almost everywhere it looks
details.description: Department of Labor investigators in the Southeast region found violations in 78% of more than 280 investigations conducted in 2020.
details.energy_note: Four in five inspected employers, in breach.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - H-2B has even less protection
details.description: Unlike H-2A, H-2B does not require employers to provide housing or court-enforceable contracts. From 2018 to 2020, 853 H-2B workers were victims of labour trafficking. In Briones v. JNS Construction Services, 69 Mexican citizens sued over forced labour, each having paid a $400 recruitment fee and $250 for travel.
details.energy_note: Six hundred and fifty dollars, to be trafficked.

details.aspect: Complaining ends the visa and the next season
details.description: The worker who reports is not rehired next season, and blacklisting travels between recruiters in the same towns.
details.energy_note: Complain once, never recruited again.

details.aspect: The recruiter is in his own town and known to his family
details.description: Recruitment happens through local intermediaries in small Mexican towns, so refusing or complaining has consequences at home, not only in the destination country.
details.energy_note: The man who recruited him drinks with his uncle.

issues.title: The corner, and being paid at the end of the day or not
issues.category_name: Work abroad: wage theft, the sponsor, the day-labour corner
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Day labour: hired from a street corner by a stranger in a truck, with no contract, no record, and no way to enforce payment.

details.aspect: The whole transaction is deniable
details.description: No name, no paperwork, no plate number written down. If he is not paid at 6pm there is nobody to pursue, and he knows that when he gets in the truck.
details.energy_note: He got in knowing there was no recourse.

details.aspect: Reporting theft means reporting himself
details.description: Wage claims require identifying himself to an agency, which for an undocumented worker is a calculation with a second column in it.
details.energy_note: The complaint form asks for his status.

details.aspect: The most dangerous jobs pay cash
details.description: Demolition, roofing, asbestos, tank cleaning - work priced high precisely because it is refused by anyone with alternatives.
details.energy_note: Paid extra for the part that may kill him.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - come back tomorrow
details.description: Eleven hours on a roof. The man says the cheque from the homeowner has not cleared, and to come back Thursday at the same corner. He comes back Thursday. He comes back the Thursday after that too.
details.energy_note: Two hundred and forty dollars, and a corner he keeps returning to.

issues.title: Named on the CV, before anyone reads it
issues.category_name: Work abroad: wage theft, the sponsor, the day-labour corner
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Name-based screening in hiring, and the accent on the phone.

details.aspect: The correspondence-study tradition
details.description: Matched-CV audit studies consistently find callback gaps by name across many labour markets. The Mexican version runs through both the surname and any indication of where schooling happened.
details.energy_note: Identical CV, different surname, fewer calls.

details.aspect: Arceo-Gómez and Campos-Vázquez did it inside Mexico
details.description: Their correspondence work on race and appearance in the Mexican labour market, and on discrimination in job advertisements and callbacks, found the sorting happens domestically too - it is not only a border phenomenon.
details.energy_note: The same filter operates at home.
details.notes: See DIS-001.

details.aspect: Qualifications are discounted across the line
details.description: A Mexican degree or trade certification is frequently treated as unverifiable abroad, pushing trained men into unskilled work and keeping them there.
details.energy_note: An engineer, framing houses.

details.aspect: SCENE - the name on the application
details.description: He applies as Jose Ramirez Delgado. Nothing. A friend suggests he try 'Joe Ramirez'. He gets two callbacks in a fortnight for the same kind of role. He does not tell anyone he did this, including his father, who chose the name.
details.energy_note: Two callbacks, and something he will not mention to his father.

issues.title: The highest workplace death rate of any group
issues.category_name: The body at work: injury, heat, height, and what it costs
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Hispanic and Latino workers in the US have had the highest fatal injury rate of any group for eight consecutive years, and most of those deaths are foreign-born men.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the rate and the streak
details.description: BLS recorded a fatal injury rate of 4.3 per 100,000 FTE for Hispanic or Latino workers in 2024, down from 4.4 in 2023 - the eighth consecutive year with the highest death rate of any group, against an all-worker rate of 3.3.
details.energy_note: Eight years running, the most likely to die at work.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and most of them are immigrants
details.description: Of the 1,229 fatalities among Hispanic or Latino workers in 2024, 68.5% - 842 - were foreign-born.
details.energy_note: Eight hundred and forty-two men who had come to work.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - construction, and a rising share
details.description: In 2021, 274 fatalities among foreign-born Hispanic or Latino workers accounted for 27% of all deaths in the construction industry, up from 19.8% in 2011. Falls, slips and trips were the most common fatal event.
details.energy_note: A quarter of everyone who dies on a site.

details.aspect: THE HONEST GAP - no rate exists for the intersection
details.description: BLS does not publish fatality rates by race or ethnicity for specific industries or occupations - only counts. So there is no published fatality rate for Hispanic construction workers specifically, and anyone quoting one has made it up.
details.energy_note: The number everyone wants does not exist.

details.aspect: Reporting the hazard is what ends the job
details.description: The man who raises the missing harness is the man not called for the next job, so the safety system depends on complaints from precisely the people who cannot afford to make them.
details.energy_note: Safety depends on a complaint he cannot afford.

issues.title: Back pain as an occupational outcome
issues.category_name: The body at work: injury, heat, height, and what it costs
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: The brief asked about back pain specifically. It is measured in Latino manual workers, and the association with job precariousness - not just lifting - is the finding that matters.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the sweet potato study
details.description: Among 120 farmworkers hand-harvesting sweet potatoes in eastern North Carolina, 79% reported any pain or discomfort; the back was highest at 66%, shoulders 31%. Working more than five years as a farmworker was significantly associated with back pain.
details.energy_note: Two in three, in the back.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - precarity predicts back pain, independently
details.description: In a study of 189 farmworkers and non-farmworkers in North Carolina, job precariousness was associated with back pain at an odds ratio of 2.09 (95% CI 1.01-4.23), and depressive symptoms were significantly associated with neck and shoulder pain.
details.energy_note: Insecure work doubles the back pain, on its own.
details.notes: This is the row that answers the brief's 'efficiency, growth, back pain' question most directly. Compare SOM-002 in assets/text/nigeria, which found the same shape in a different population.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - non-farm manual work is worse, not better
details.description: Physician examinations of 272 workers found musculoskeletal disorders in 49% of non-farmworkers against 35% of farmworkers, with epicondylitis 20.2% and rotator cuff syndrome 19.1%. Overall prevalence was high compared with other workers in similar occupations.
details.energy_note: Leaving the fields does not save the body.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and it feeds straight back into output
details.description: A Texas study of 228 workers across 28 small construction firms found musculoskeletal pain and sleep hours significantly affected productivity, with more pain sites producing more severe productivity loss, worst among those sleeping under six hours.
details.energy_note: The pain, then the output, then the earnings.

details.aspect: Treated late, because treatment costs a day
details.description: Pain is worked through until it is disabling, because a clinic visit costs a shift and possibly the job - so the presentation is chronic by the time it is seen.
details.energy_note: Seen by a doctor years after it started.

details.aspect: The body is the asset and it is depreciating
details.description: Where earning depends on lifting, the working life is finite and the end of it arrives around fifty with no pension attached - ECO-001's informality means no contributions were made.
details.energy_note: The asset wears out at fifty and there is no pension.

details.aspect: He teaches his son the same trade
details.description: Without the credential route (PSY-005), the transmissible asset is the trade itself, so the occupational exposure is inherited along with the livelihood.
details.energy_note: Passing on the work and the back pain together.

issues.title: Heat
issues.category_name: The body at work: injury, heat, height, and what it costs
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Outdoor work in rising temperatures, with water, shade and rest breaks contested rather than guaranteed.

details.aspect: Piece rates punish pausing
details.description: Where pay is per bucket, per box or per row, a break is a pay cut, so the incentive runs directly against the safety advice.
details.energy_note: Resting costs him by the bucket.

details.aspect: Chronic kidney disease of unknown origin
details.description: Repeated heat stress and dehydration in agricultural labour is associated with kidney damage in Mesoamerican working populations - an illness of the job rather than of any single accident.
details.energy_note: Kidneys, at forty, from the heat.

details.aspect: Protection varies by state and by administration
details.description: Heat standards exist in some jurisdictions and not others, and change with politics, so the same work is regulated or not depending on which side of a state line it happens.
details.energy_note: Legal protection that stops at the county line.

details.aspect: SCENE - paid by the bucket
details.description: It is 41 degrees. The water is at the end of the row, four minutes' walk each way. Eight minutes is most of a bucket, and a bucket is $2.20. He works out he can afford to drink twice more before lunch.
details.energy_note: Doing arithmetic on how many times he can afford to drink.

issues.title: Sixty billion dollars, and what it costs to send it
issues.category_name: Remittances: the money sent, and what sending it costs
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Mexican nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Remittances are the visible product of the whole arrangement. The flow is enormous, the fees are a levy on the poorest transfers, and in 2025 it fell for the first time in over a decade.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the size, and the turn
details.description: Mexico received $61.79bn in family remittances in 2025, a 4.6% year-on-year fall - the first annual contraction after eleven consecutive years of growth and the biggest drop since 2009. The record was 2024 at $64.7bn across 164.8m transactions.
details.energy_note: Sixty-two billion dollars, and falling.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - what it is worth to the country
details.description: Remittances were about 3.4% of Mexican GDP in 2025. Guanajuato was the largest recipient state at $5.51bn, 8.9% of the national total. Electronic transfer accounted for 99.1%.
details.energy_note: Three and a half per cent of the economy, sent home in pieces.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the money shrank even where it arrived
details.description: The peso appreciated 10.2% against the dollar between November 2024 and November 2025; with inflation, the real purchasing power of remittances fell 14.4% year-on-year in November for 4.4m receiving households.
details.energy_note: Same dollars, a seventh less food.

details.aspect: The fee is a tax on being poor and far away
details.description: Transfer costs fall hardest on small, frequent transfers, which is the pattern used by people sending part of a weekly wage.
details.money_note: Annual fees on regular small transfers.
details.energy_note: Charged most per dollar for sending the fewest.

details.aspect: Sending it is also how he stays a father
details.description: The transfer is the relationship: it is proof of continued presence, and missing one is read at home as something other than a bad month.
details.energy_note: The month he sends nothing means something else entirely.

details.aspect: The 2025 fall is an enforcement indicator
details.description: Analysts attributed much of the drop to US immigration policy change, with DHS data suggesting border crossings down 93% year-on-year in 2025. The remittance line is therefore a proxy for how many men are managing to be there at all.
details.energy_note: The money falling is the men not arriving.

issues.title: The one who left, and what he is now for
issues.category_name: Remittances: the money sent, and what sending it costs
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Being the household's income from a distance reorganises a man's place in his own family into a function.

details.aspect: Requests arrive as news
details.description: The roof, the operation, the cousin's wedding, the school fees. Each is real, and collectively they are a claim on everything he earns, forever.
details.energy_note: Every phone call has a number in it.

details.aspect: Saying no is the same as abandoning them
details.description: Declining a request is not heard as a budget limit but as a statement about the family, so refusing costs standing rather than money.
details.energy_note: No is not a financial answer, it is a moral one.

details.aspect: He is envied and he is broke
details.description: The village version of his life is dollars; the actual version is a shared room and a bus pass. Both are true and only one travels.
details.energy_note: Rich at home, sleeping four to a room.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - the photograph of the house
details.description: They send him a picture of the second storey he paid for. He has never stood in it, and cannot, because of VIS-003. He sets it as his phone background.
details.energy_note: A house he owns and has never entered.

issues.title: More than half the workforce is informal
issues.category_name: The informal economy, the wage, and the length of the day
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Mexico, any gender
issues.summary: Informality is not a fringe - it is the majority condition of Mexican work, and it means no contract, no social security and no pension.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the rate, and that it never moves
details.description: INEGI recorded informality at 55.1% in Q2 2026, up from 54.8%, with 54.78% in Q1 2026 covering 32.63 million people. The share has been essentially stagnant for two decades and remains above 50%.
details.energy_note: Twenty years of reform, and the number does not move.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the unemployment rate is a decoy
details.description: Mexican unemployment was reported at 2.4% - the lowest in the OECD - alongside very high informality and slow formal job growth. Almost everyone works; the question is under what terms.
details.energy_note: Full employment, and no contracts.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and a rising share earn at or below minimum
details.description: Nearly 27.9 million people earn the minimum wage or less - 45.7% of the employed population, an annual increase of 4.3 million. INEGI's critical employment conditions rate rose from 36.3% in May 2025 to 38.7% in May 2026.
details.energy_note: Nearly half the workforce, at or under the floor.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the wage did rise, substantially
details.description: The daily minimum wage reached MX$315.04 in most of the country and MX$440.87 in the northern border zone on 1 January 2026, a 13% increase, with the federal minimum up more than 100% in real terms since 2018. This is recorded because it is real and unusual.
details.energy_note: It genuinely doubled, and it is still this.

issues.title: Second in the OECD for hours worked
issues.category_name: The informal economy, the wage, and the length of the day
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Mexico, any gender
issues.summary: The Mexican working year is among the longest in the developed world, which is the hidden term in every comparison of Mexican wages to anyone else's.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the ranking and the stability
details.description: Mexico ranks second in the OECD for hours worked per year, and average weekly hours have stayed around 42-43 for the last twenty years.
details.energy_note: Second in the developed world, for twenty years.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the 40-hour week keeps being proposed
details.description: Both the 2018-24 and 2024-30 administrations pushed a constitutional reform to cut the week from 48 to 40 hours and increase paid holidays. It remains a proposal rather than a condition of anyone's life.
details.energy_note: Two governments have promised it.

details.aspect: The commute is not in the number
details.description: Hours worked exclude two to four hours a day travelling from the periphery of Mexico City, Monterrey or Guadalajara, which is time gone from the same day.
details.energy_note: Fourteen hours away from the house, for eight paid.

details.aspect: What it leaves for anything else
details.description: Long hours plus commuting plus a second job is why the goodlife dataset's `time` trigger bites hardest here: the good things that require an evening are the ones that do not happen.
details.energy_note: No hours left in which to have a life.
details.notes: Interacts with the `time`/`work` triggers in assets/text/goodlife.

issues.title: Nine in ten of the dead are men
issues.category_name: Homicide and armed violence, and who it actually kills
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Mexican homicide is overwhelmingly the killing of young men. The figure is stable across three decades and is the single most important number in this dataset.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the 2023 split
details.description: Of 31,062 homicide victims in Mexico in 2023 (INEGI preliminary), 27,221 were men and 3,578 women - 87.6% against 11.5%, with 263 unspecified.
details.energy_note: Twenty-seven thousand men, in one year.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and across thirty-three years
details.description: A study of INEGI mortality data covering 605,260 homicides from 1990 to 2022 found 538,996 - 89.05% - were male. The age-adjusted rate for men in 2022 was 41.55 per 100,000 against 5.48 for women.
details.energy_note: Half a million men, over three decades.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - concentrated in young adulthood
details.description: In firearm mortality analysis, one third of victims were aged 20-29, though rates among children and adolescents rose at a faster proportional pace.
details.energy_note: A third of them in their twenties.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Mexico's male share exceeds the world's
details.description: UNODC's 2023 Global Study on Homicide found 81% of homicide victims worldwide were men in 2021. Mexico runs several points above that.
details.energy_note: Even by world standards, unusually male.

details.aspect: Where it happens differs by sex, which matters
details.description: Nearly one in five female homicides occur in the home, against one in thirteen for male homicides. Male killing tracks organised crime; female killing has a weaker relationship to it and more often involves intimate partners. These are two different problems with one statistic.
details.energy_note: He dies in the street, she dies in the house.
details.notes: Recorded deliberately so this dataset cannot be read as diminishing femicide. Different mechanisms, both real.

details.aspect: The counting itself is contested
details.description: INEGI builds from death certificates via the mortality registry, capturing homicides never formally investigated, which is why its count exceeds SESNSP's every year. Two official numbers exist and they do not agree.
details.energy_note: Two government counts, neither wrong.

details.aspect: Life expectancy actually fell
details.description: Male life expectancy in Mexico stalled and reversed during the peak violence years - an effect large enough to move a national demographic indicator, which is rare outside war.
details.energy_note: Enough killing to shorten the national lifespan.

details.aspect: Every man in the family has a story
details.description: At these rates the violence is not statistical for anyone - a cousin, a neighbour, a schoolfriend - so the fear is memory rather than anticipation.
details.energy_note: Not afraid of what might happen. Remembering.

issues.title: Being the demographic
issues.category_name: Homicide and armed violence, and who it actually kills
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: A young man in certain states is read by police, employers, landlords and border officers as a member of a category before he is read as a person - by the same statistics that describe him as the likeliest victim.

details.aspect: The same number, used both ways
details.description: That young men are overwhelmingly the victims is also used as grounds to treat young men as the threat. He is inside the statistic in both directions at once.
details.energy_note: The number that describes his danger describes him as dangerous.

details.aspect: Dress, tattoos, vehicle, hour
details.description: A truck, a cap, visible ink and being out late constitute reasonable suspicion in practice if not in law, which makes ordinary young-man behaviour into a profile.
details.energy_note: Suspicious for being twenty-four and outdoors.

details.aspect: He adapts his own life pre-emptively
details.description: Routes changed, hours shortened, clothing chosen for how it reads, phone kept visible - a continuous unpaid management of other people's suspicion.
details.energy_note: Dressing every morning for a police officer.

details.aspect: SCENE - the long way round
details.description: There is a direct road home that takes eleven minutes. He takes the one that takes twenty-six, because the direct one passes two places where young men get stopped. He has done this every night for three years and has never once described it as fear.
details.energy_note: Fifteen extra minutes, nightly, that he does not call fear.

issues.title: The reporter who is killed for the story
issues.category_name: Homicide and armed violence, and who it actually kills
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Mexico, any gender
issues.summary: Mexico is repeatedly ranked among the deadliest countries on earth for journalists, and the killing is mostly unsolved.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the toll since 2000
details.description: Article 19 has documented at least 174 murders and 31 disappearances of journalists in Mexico since 2000. Counts differ by methodology - Article 19 listed 157 killings 2000-2022 while the Atlantic Council's count gave 163.
details.energy_note: A hundred and seventy-four, and counting.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the worst year, and the ranking
details.description: 2022 was the deadliest year, with 13 killings per CPJ and Article 19 - the Atlantic Council counted 18. RSF ranked Mexico the deadliest country for the press three consecutive years, and second worldwide in 2025 with at least nine killed.
details.energy_note: Worst in the world, three years running.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - most attacks are by officials, not cartels
details.description: Contrary to the cartel-centric assumption, Article 19 found 42% of attacks on the press are committed by government officials, ahead of criminal actors and private entities. In 2022 Mexico recorded an attack on journalists or media houses every 13 hours.
details.energy_note: The state is the single largest attacker.

details.aspect: Impunity is the operative fact
details.description: All but a handful of killings and abductions of media workers remain unsolved. Veracruz is the deadliest state.
details.energy_note: Almost none of them are ever solved.

issues.title: Over a hundred thousand people, not found
issues.category_name: Disappearance, the searching, and the graves
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Mexico's registry of disappeared and missing persons is among the largest in the world outside active warfare, and roughly three quarters of it is men.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the totals, with their disagreements
details.description: The RNPDNO recorded roughly 367,392 disappearances since 1952 as of July 2025, of whom 237,382 were located and 130,010 remain missing. A March 2026 government update cited 394,645 records, with 262,111 located - 240,211 alive and 21,900 dead. La Jornada reported 132,534 disappeared, most from the last twenty years.
details.energy_note: Somewhere above a hundred and thirty thousand.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the sex split
details.description: The IACHR reported that of 128,713 people registered as disappeared as of 3 June 2025, 76.83% were men. Red Lupa found the split stable between May 2022 and May 2025. State variation is wide - Sinaloa 92%, Jalisco 86%.
details.energy_note: Three quarters of the missing are men.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and they are young
details.description: Men aged 20-34 and women aged 19-24 are the most frequently disappeared groups; people aged 20-34 accounted for at least 30,548 cases, about 40% of the total in one cut of the data. Recent reporting indicates the average age is falling, with 15-19 year olds now leading.
details.energy_note: Twenty to thirty-four, and getting younger.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the registry is contested
details.description: The official count is 'depurada' - cleaned - and it is estimated that for every reported disappearance there are at least 1.5 never brought to prosecutors, largely from fear of reprisals. One source reports the 2025 sex split shifting to 62.84% men, against the historic 76-77%. The number is a political object as well as a statistic.
details.energy_note: The count is itself disputed, annually.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the concentration
details.description: Jalisco, Estado de México, Tamaulipas, Veracruz and Nuevo León account for 44.3% of cases; Jalisco alone had 15,330. Active cases of young men concentrate in Jalisco, Estado de México and Chihuahua.
details.energy_note: Five states hold nearly half of it.

details.aspect: Ambiguous loss has no ritual
details.description: Without a body there is no funeral, no inheritance, no remarriage and no end to searching. The family is suspended indefinitely in a state with no social script for it.
details.energy_note: No funeral, no death certificate, no permission to stop.

details.aspect: Declaring him dead is required to get anything and feels like betrayal
details.description: Accessing accounts, property or benefits requires a declaration of absence or death, so the administrative system forces the family to give up before they are ready.
details.energy_note: Asked to sign that her son is dead, to pay his mortgage.

issues.title: The mothers who dig
issues.category_name: Disappearance, the searching, and the graves
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Mexico, any gender
issues.summary: Because the state does not search effectively, families - mostly mothers and sisters of missing men - search themselves, with rods and shovels, and find the graves.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - a collective found the Jalisco ranch
details.description: Rancho Izaguirre in Teuchitlán was uncovered on 5 March 2025 by Guerreros Buscadores, a civilian collective of families searching for missing people - not by any state agency.
details.energy_note: Volunteers found it. Not the state.

details.aspect: The searchers are themselves killed
details.description: Members of search collectives have been murdered for searching. The work is done by relatives because it is not done otherwise, and it carries the same risk that produced the disappearance.
details.energy_note: Killed for looking for her son.

details.aspect: The inversion this dataset is built on
details.description: The disappeared are overwhelmingly men; the people searching are overwhelmingly women. The violence is gendered in both directions at once and the two facts belong together.
details.energy_note: Men vanish; women look for them.
details.notes: Cross-reference to assets/text/nigeria and palestine, which hold the women-first view of the same structures.

details.aspect: VILLAIN SCENE - the rod
details.description: She pushes a steel rod into the ground and pulls it out and smells it. That is the method. She has done this on seventy Saturdays. The state prosecutor's office has sent someone twice.
details.energy_note: Seventy Saturdays, and a smell on a metal rod.

issues.title: Ayotzinapa: forty-three, and a state that lied about it
issues.category_name: Disappearance, the searching, and the graves
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: The disappearance of 43 male students in 2014, the fabricated official account, and a decade of confirmed obstruction - the case that demonstrates what happens when a disappearance is too big to bury.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - what happened
details.description: On 26 September 2014, 43 students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers' College were forcibly disappeared in Iguala, Guerrero. They had left to take part in a demonstration commemorating the 2 October 1968 student massacre.
details.energy_note: Forty-three young men, on their way to a commemoration.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the 'historical truth' was built on torture
details.description: The Peña Nieto government closed the case within months on confessions that the bodies were burned in a dump. International experts disputed it, citing confessions obtained by torture, illegal arrests of key suspects and absence of physical evidence. The GIEI, appointed by the IACHR in 2015, rejected the cremation theory as physically impossible as described.
details.energy_note: The official story was produced by torturing people.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the state later admitted it was a state crime
details.description: The truth commission report released on 18 August 2022 conceded the disappearance was a 'state crime' involving local officials and military units, and that the previous government pursued deliberate concealment and obstruction. Critics noted it did not address the roles of SEDENA, the military command or CISEN.
details.energy_note: Admitted as a state crime, with the state's own part left out.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and the files are still being fought for
details.description: The GIEI completed its work on 31 July 2023. A federal judge ruled the army must make public 853 files obtained in 2014 by the Regional Intelligence Fusion Center, after parents filed an amparo in 2023 against the military for violating the 2018 decree creating the truth commission.
details.energy_note: Twelve years on, still suing for the documents.

details.aspect: Nine years on, the IACHR recorded nothing resolved
details.description: Whereabouts not determined, facts not fully clarified, those responsible not punished. The most internationally scrutinised disappearance in Mexican history is unsolved - which sets the expectation for all the others.
details.energy_note: If this one is unsolved, none of them will be.

issues.title: The job advertisement that is a trap
issues.category_name: Cartels: recruitment, forced labour and the fake job ad
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Mexican nationality and being male
issues.summary: Forced recruitment of young men through fake job postings offering security work at above-market pay - the mechanism uncovered at Teuchitlán in 2025.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the method
details.description: Recruiters posted fake job ads on social media, typically offering security guard positions paying MX$4,000-12,000 weekly (roughly US$200-600) - well above market. Applicants were told to gather at designated bus terminals and were transported to Rancho Izaguirre. Authorities identified at least 60 pages used for this.
details.energy_note: A good wage, a bus station, and a van.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - many did not know who was hiring
details.description: While some listings advertised CJNG positions openly, many survivors reported being unaware of cartel involvement until they arrived. A reported survivor described being picked up at a bus station under false pretences and trained for a month in weapons and fitness; those who refused or tried to escape were beaten, tortured and killed.
details.energy_note: He thought he was going to a guard job.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the site
details.description: The ranch, known as 'La Escuelita', contained human remains and over 400 items of clothing, plus bone fragments and hundreds of shoes. Federal officials later said they had not verified mass incinerations beyond one body - an investigative gap recorded here rather than resolved.
details.energy_note: Four hundred sets of clothes, and a dispute about the ovens.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - it was not the first sign
details.description: In 2024, 30 young people disappeared after attending fake job interviews in San Pedro Tlaquepaque, Jalisco.
details.energy_note: Thirty, the year before, the same way.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - arrests, collusion and sentences
details.description: José Gregorio Lastra, 'El Comandante Lastra', allegedly in charge of CJNG recruitment, was arrested on 24 March 2025. The Teuchitlán mayor was detained in May 2025 and local police were flagged. In July 2025 a court sentenced 10 men to 141 years each for crimes linked to the ranch.
details.energy_note: A mayor, the police, and 141 years each.

details.aspect: Most recruitment is not forced, which is the harder fact
details.description: Experts describe three routes: volunteers drawn by pay and status - the bulk of members - targeted recruitment of ex-military and police as trainers, and forced recruitment. The DEA estimates CJNG at around 19,000 members. For a young man with ECO-001's options, the offer is rational.
details.energy_note: For most of them it was the best job available.

details.aspect: The advertisement is still findable
details.description: The postings are ordinary-looking job ads on ordinary platforms, which is what makes the warning impossible to give usefully: there is no visible marker distinguishing the trap from the real vacancy.
details.energy_note: It looks exactly like a job advert, because it is one.

details.aspect: Why he answered it
details.description: ECO-001's minimum wage against MX$4,000-12,000 a week explains the response rate entirely. The recruitment works because the legitimate economy offers him less.
details.energy_note: Four times the legal wage, and he has a daughter.

issues.title: Taxed by whoever holds the road
issues.category_name: Cartels: recruitment, forced labour and the fake job ad
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Mexico, any gender
issues.summary: Territorial control exercised as a levy on movement and trade - the closest thing in this dataset to the brief's word 'occupied'.

details.aspect: Control without occupation
details.description: Large regions operate under de facto armed authority that collects, permits and punishes. It is not a foreign occupation and it is not the state either.
details.energy_note: Somebody governs the road, and it is not the government.
details.notes: This row is why the build script corrects 'occupied Mexico' rather than simply rejecting the brief's word.
